analysis.one_liner: Stops employers from stripping pension and health benefits by relabeling workers as temps or contractors.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with three backers in June 2007, sent to a House committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the federal law governing private pension and health plans (ERISA) to stop employers from denying benefits to workers by labeling them as temporary, part-time, leased, agency, staffing-firm, or independent-contractor workers when they actually do the same work as regular employees. It counted all service toward benefit eligibility regardless of how the worker was paid, barred plans from excluding workers based on labels alone, blocked forced waivers of benefit rights, and gave workers stronger tools — including back pay, reinstatement, and automatic attorney's fees — to sue when employers disciplined them for asserting those rights. It never got past a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who do the same work as regular employees but are labeled temps, leased employees, agency workers, staffing-firm employees, or independent contractors, and who are therefore locked out of the employer's pension and welfare benefit plans. The bill would have credited their service and required plans to include them, barred employers from forcing them to sign away benefit rights as a condition of keeping their job, and made it easier and cheaper to sue over violations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Misclassified temp, leased, and contract workers

how_it_helps.text: Requires that all service for the employer count toward pension eligibility regardless of whether the worker was paid through a staffing firm, temp agency, payroll agency, or from a non-payroll account, and counts service performed after a forced reclassification.

Bars pension plans from excluding anyone who performs the same or substantially the same work as employees who are generally in the plan, no matter what worker category the plan uses to exclude them, and requires plan eligibility rules to be uniform and based on objective criteria rather than labels.
Provides that a worker forced to convert to temp, leased, agency, or contractor status as a condition of continued employment does not lose plan participation because of the conversion.

Lets courts award compensatory and remedial relief, restitution, reinstatement, and back pay with lost benefits to workers excluded or misclassified in violation of the rules, and requires courts to award attorney's fees to prevailing workers in these cases.

Makes rights under the law non-waivable by default: waivers of benefit-plan rights are void unless knowing and voluntary, agreed after a dispute arose or through a union contract, with the employer bearing the burden of proof and no requirement that a worker give back severance before challenging a waiver in court.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that use staffing firms, employee-leasing arrangements, and contractor labels to keep workers out of benefit plans would have had to enroll them, pay the benefit costs, and restructure plan eligibility. Temporary staffing and employee-leasing firms would lose part of their value proposition. Plan sponsors and fiduciaries would face new compliance and potential litigation costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers using contingent labor to dodge benefits

drawbacks.text: The bill sweeps broadly: it applies to any worker doing 'substantially the same work' as plan-covered employees, which employers argued could force the inclusion of genuine independent contractors and short-term staff and raise benefit costs well beyond cases of true misclassification.

It would create new litigation exposure for plan sponsors and fiduciaries by expanding remedies to compensatory and remedial relief, mandating attorney's fees for prevailing workers in these cases, and letting courts treat plan-level exclusion provisions as invalid.

Even employers acting in good faith would bear administrative costs, since plan documents must be rewritten with objective, uniform eligibility criteria and collectively bargained plans could not adjust until after existing contracts expire.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers directly affected — people doing the same work as colleagues but stripped of retirement and health benefits through labels and paperwork — the gains are substantial and concrete. The costs fall on a narrower set of employers and staffing firms whose business model depends on keeping those workers off the benefit rolls, plus some compliance burden on all plan sponsors. The main honest objection is drafting breadth: rules keyed to 'substantially the same work' are hard to administer and would likely have been narrowed through negotiation. That kind of trade-off is normally worked out in committee; here it never got the chance.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee in June 2007, then to a subcommittee a month later, and died there — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, ever.

narrative.text: Representative Carolyn McCarthy of New York introduced the Employee Benefits Protection Act of 2007 on June 11, 2007, joined by Representatives Lynn Woolsey and Dale Kildee.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor on the day of introduction.
On July 24, 2007, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions, and no further action was taken for the rest of the 110th Congress.
The bill never received a vote in the House or Senate and expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and staffing firms that keep workers out of pension and health plans through temp, leased, and contractor labels keep that option; no worker gained the bill's protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and staffing firms kept the status quo

for.name: Rep. Carolyn McCarthy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its case that mislabeling workers to strip benefits violates ERISA.

for.name: 2 of 2 House cosponsors
for.role: Original cosponsors (Reps. Lynn Woolsey and Dale Kildee)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no other members joined.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Rep. George Miller, D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, passed it to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions on July 24, 2007, and never held a markup or advanced it.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's only support came from three House Democrats, and no Republican cosponsor signed on, so the partisan shape is visible only in the absence of Republican backing and the majority party's decision not to move it.

industries.industry: Temporary staffing, employee leasing, and payroll agencies
industries.note: These firms exist in part to place workers with a client while keeping them off the client's benefit rolls. The bill would have counted their placements as service for benefits and barred label-based exclusions, removing a core selling point.

industries.industry: Employers relying on contingent labor to avoid benefit costs
industries.note: Employers that classify workers as temps, leased employees, or contractors to keep them out of pension and welfare plans would have had to enroll them and pay for their benefits.

industries.industry: Benefit plan sponsors, fiduciaries, and administrators
industries.note: Plan documents would need rewritten, objective eligibility rules and fiduciaries would face more litigation exposure, but the rules mainly target employers using labels to exclude same-work employees rather than the plan administration business itself.
